title: How common are overuse injuries?
goal: Define overuse injury, read incidence per 1000 h, and say which risk factors the cohort evidence supports and how firmly.

steps.title: What counts as an overuse injury
steps.text:
An [overuse injury](g:overuse-injury) has no single moment of injury: damage builds up over many loads, then pain starts. That makes it hard to count. Is a runner injured if she trains through knee pain at half her usual distance?

Researchers agreed a definition for runners: lower-limb pain from running that restricts or stops running for at least 7 days or 3 scheduled sessions in a row, or that needs a health professional [[c:ie-def]].

Counting only [time-loss injuries](g:time-loss-injury) misses most problems. In a 13-week study of 313 athletes, standard records found 40 overuse injuries of the knee, lower back and shoulder; weekly questionnaires found 419 problems there [[c:ie-undercount]].

claims.text: A Delphi panel agreed a definition of running-related injury: lower-limb pain that restricts or stops running for at least 7 days or 3 consecutive scheduled sessions, or that needs a health professional.

evidence.quote: Running-related (training or competition) musculoskeletal pain in the lower limbs that causes a restriction on or stoppage of running (distance, speed, duration, or training) for at least 7 days or 3 consecutive scheduled training sessions, or that requires the runner to consult a physician or other health professional.

claims.text: Time-loss records capture only a small share of overuse problems, because few problems lead to time loss.

evidence.quote: Standard injury surveillance methods only capture a small percentage of the overuse problems affecting the athletes, largely because few problems led to time loss from training or competition.

steps.title: Incidence: injuries per 1000 hours
steps.text:
To compare groups, set injuries against exposure. [Incidence](g:incidence) = new injuries ÷ hours run × 1000. Counting per runner misleads: someone who runs 10 h a year has far less chance of injury than someone who runs 300 h.

Pooled results from prospective studies [[c:ie-rates]]:

| runners | injuries per 1000 h |
|---|---|
| novice | 17.8 |
| recreational | 7.7 |

Single studies ranged from 2.5 (long-distance track athletes) to 33.0 (novices). Studies used different injury definitions, so compare with care.

claims.text: Pooled incidence of running-related injury was 17.8 per 1000 h in novice runners and 7.7 in recreational runners.

evidence.quote: The meta-analyses revealed a weighted injury incidence of 17.8 (95% confidence interval [CI] 16.7-19.1) in novice runners and 7.7 (95% CI 6.9-8.7) in recreational runners.
Heterogeneity in definitions of injury, definition of type of runner, and outcome measures in the included full-text articles challenged comparison across studies.
Running-related injuries per 1000 h of running ranged from a minimum of 2.5 in a study of long-distance track and field athletes to a maximum of 33.0 in a study of novice runners.

steps.title: Incidence from raw counts
steps.problem: Forty runners log 12 injuries while running 1500 h in total. What is the incidence per 1000 h?

steps.title: Cyclists and triathletes
steps.text:
Cyclists and triathletes also get overuse injuries, but the data are thinner. In 109 professional road cyclists asked about the last 12 months, 94 injuries were registered: 45% in the lower back and 23% in the knee. Of 23 time-loss injuries, 57% were in the knee [[c:ie-cyclists]].

Of 758 Brazilian triathletes, 425 (56%) reported an injury in the past 12 months, mostly in the lower limbs, the knee most often [[c:ie-triathletes]].

Both rest on memory of the past year, and the triathlete data came from an online form. A share of people over a year is not a rate per 1000 h, so 56% can't be set next to 17.8.

claims.text: In professional road cyclists, overuse injuries were mostly in the lower back (45%) and knee (23%); the knee caused most time-loss injuries (57%).

evidence.quote: A total of 94 injuries were registered; 45% were in the lower back and 23% in the knee.
Twenty-three time-loss injuries were registered-57% in the knee, 22% in the lower back, and 13% in the lower leg.

claims.text: In a survey of 758 triathletes, 425 reported an injury in the past 12 months, mostly in the lower limbs and most often the knee.

evidence.quote: More than half (n = 425) reported an injury in the past 12 months, most frequently in the lower limbs, particularly the knee (16.88%).

steps.title: Risk factors: previous injury and training errors
steps.text:
Which factors predict injury? A review of 11 prospective cohorts (4,671 runners) found one main factor: an injury in the previous 12 months [[c:ie-prev]]. Only one had a random sample, and only six followed runners for 6 months or more.

Training errors are plausible but less certain. Among 874 novices, those who raised weekly distance by more than 30% over 2 weeks had a [hazard ratio](g:hazard-ratio) (HR, a rate ratio) of 1.59 for distance-related injuries against those who raised it by under 10%. The [95% CI](g:confidence-interval) was 0.96–2.66; the authors called the study exploratory. A systematic review found very limited evidence for a link between sudden load change and injury [[c:ie-prog]].

The critique of the acute:chronic ratio is in the ACWR lesson, not repeated here.

claims.text: The main risk factor for running injury found in prospective cohorts was an injury in the previous 12 months.

evidence.quote: The main risk factor identified in this review was previous injury in the last 12 months, although many risk factors had been investigated in the literature.
Only one article met the criteria for random selection of the sample and only six articles included a follow-up of 6 months or more.

claims.text: Large jumps in running distance may raise injury rates, but the evidence is limited and exploratory.

evidence.quote: Novice runners who progressed their running distance by more than 30% over a 2-week period seem to be more vulnerable to distance-related injuries than runners who increase their running distance by less than 10%.
Very limited evidence exists supporting that a sudden change in training load is associated with increased risk of running-related injury.

points: An overuse injury builds up from repeated load; a good definition counts restricted training, not just missed sessions.
Incidence per 1000 h puts exposure in the bottom line: pooled rates were 17.8 for novice and 7.7 for recreational runners.
Cyclists mostly report lower back and knee problems, triathletes knee and other lower-limb ones: both from recall and surveys.
Previous injury is the best-supported risk factor; training errors are plausible, but the evidence is thin.

variants.stem: What separates an overuse injury from an acute injury?

options.text: It builds up over many loads, with no single moment of injury
options.why: Right: repeated loading adds up until pain starts.

options.text: It only affects tendons, since they are loaded again and again
options.why: Bone, muscle and other tissues get overuse injuries too.

options.text: It always stops the athlete from training for a week
options.why: Many overuse injuries are trained through; time loss is not part of the idea.

options.text: It is caused by poor technique and nothing else
options.why: Technique is one possible cause; load, tissue capacity and other factors also count.

variants.stem: A runner has had shin pain for 10 days. She still does every scheduled session but halves her usual distance. Under the consensus definition, is this a running-related injury?

options.text: Yes: pain has restricted her running for at least 7 days
options.why: Right: a cut in distance for 7 days or more counts as a restriction.

options.text: No: she missed no scheduled session
options.why: Time loss is not needed; restricted distance, speed or duration is enough.

options.text: No: she has not consulted a health professional
options.why: Seeing a professional is an alternative route, not a requirement.

options.text: Only if a scan shows damage in the shin
options.why: The definition rests on pain and its effect on running, not on imaging.

variants.stem: Why do time-loss records undercount overuse problems?

options.text: Many athletes train through pain, so no time is lost
options.why: Right: few problems cause time loss, so they never enter the records.

options.text: Athletes usually hide their pain from coaches and doctors
options.why: Hiding happens, but the study found the main gap is the definition, not secrecy.

options.text: Overuse problems are too rare to show up in a season
options.why: Weekly questionnaires found 39% of athletes with overuse problems each week.

options.text: Time loss is only logged for sudden, acute injuries
options.why: Time-loss records can include overuse injuries; they just miss the milder ones.

variants.stem: A running club logs 18 injuries over 1200 h of running by its members. What is the incidence per 1000 h?

options.why: Inverts the fraction: 1200 ÷ 18 is hours per injury.
Scales to 100 h, not 1000 h.
Forgets to multiply by 1000.

variants.stem: A triathlon squad logs 9 injuries over 1500 h of running. What is the incidence per 1000 h?

options.why: Inverts the fraction: 1500 ÷ 9 is hours per injury.
Scales to 100 h, not 1000 h.
Forgets to multiply by 1000.

variants.stem: A novice running group logs 30 injuries over 1250 h of running. What is the incidence per 1000 h?

options.why: Inverts the fraction: 1250 ÷ 30 is hours per injury.
Scales to 100 h, not 1000 h.
Forgets to multiply by 1000.

variants.stem: Why do studies give injuries per 1000 h instead of injuries per runner?

options.text: It makes groups with different running time comparable
options.why: Right: exposure is in the bottom line, so more hours no longer look like more risk.

options.text: It turns every overuse problem into a time-loss injury
options.why: The unit says nothing about how an injury is defined.

options.text: It removes the effect of age and sex on injury
options.why: Rates per hour do not adjust for who the runners are.

options.text: It gives a higher, more cautious figure for each runner
options.why: The figure is not higher by design; it just changes the unit.

variants.stem: Club A: 40 runners, 20 injuries, 8000 h run in total. Club B: 40 runners, 20 injuries, 4000 h run in total. Which statement fits?

options.text: Club A is worse: it logged more hours in total
options.why: More hours is more exposure, not more risk; it lowers A's rate.

options.text: The clubs are equal: both had 0.5 injuries per runner
options.why: Per runner ignores exposure; B ran half as many hours for the same injuries.

options.text: Club B is worse: 5.0 per 1000 h against 2.5 for Club A
Neither can be judged without the runners' ages
options.why: Age matters for risk factors, but incidence can be compared on exposure alone.

variants.stem: A pro team doctor wants to cut missed races from overuse injuries. Where should she look first?

options.text: The lower back, which had the most overuse injuries overall
options.why: Most frequent overall (45%), but only 22% of the time-loss injuries.

options.text: The shoulder, since cyclists load the arms on the bars
options.why: The shoulder was not among the main regions in this study.

options.text: The knee, which caused most time-loss injuries
options.why: Right: 57% of the 23 time-loss injuries were in the knee.

options.text: The lower leg, which is hit hardest in runners
options.why: Only 13% of the time-loss injuries in these cyclists were in the lower leg.

variants.stem: One study reports 17.8 injuries per 1000 h in novice runners. Another finds 56% of triathletes injured in the past year. A coach says triathletes get hurt far more. Best reply?

options.text: Agree: 56% is far higher than 17.8
options.why: Different units: a share of people over a year, against a rate per hour.

options.text: The numbers measure different things, so they can't be compared
options.why: Right: one is a 12-month share of people, the other a rate per exposure hour.

options.text: Agree, because triathletes also swim and cycle
options.why: Extra sports add exposure but cannot be read from these two numbers.

options.text: Disagree: triathletes train fewer hours, so risk is lower
options.why: Hours are not given in either number; this guesses at a result.

variants.stem: In prospective cohorts of runners, which risk factor was reported most often?

options.text: An injury in the previous 12 months
options.why: Right: reported in 5 of the 8 studies that looked at it.

options.text: Being female
options.why: Most studies found no link between sex and running injury.

options.text: Running more than 50 km a week
options.why: Distance was studied, but it was not the main factor found.

options.text: Being over 40 years old
options.why: Age was among many factors tested but was not the main one.

variants.stem: In 874 novice runners, raising weekly distance by over 30% gave a hazard ratio of 1.59 (95% CI 0.96–2.66) for distance-related injury. Which conclusion fits?

options.text: It proves that rises over 30% cause injury
options.why: A CI that reaches 0.96 is compatible with no effect, and cohorts cannot prove cause.

options.text: It proves rises over 30% are safe, as the CI includes 1
options.why: The CI also reaches 2.66; it cannot rule out a large rise in risk.

options.text: It is useless, as the P value is above .05
options.why: The estimate is imprecise but still informative; the authors called it exploratory.

options.text: It is suggestive: the data fit no effect or a large one
options.why: Right: wide interval, exploratory study, so more trials are needed.
